title: The physiology of forager hydration and variation among harvester ant (Pogonomyrmex barbatus) colonies in collective foraging behavior

abstract: Red harvester ant colonies must spend water to obtain water: colonies lose water as workers forage outside the nest, and gain water through seeds collected. Here we present field experiments showing that hydrated Pogonomyrmex barbatus foragers made more foraging trips than unhydrated nestmates. Desiccation tests showed that foragers of colonies that reduce foraging in dry conditions are more sensitive to water loss. methods.name: Field hydration manipulation of marked P. barbatus foragers
methods.description: Foragers from five colonies were cold-anesthetized, paint-marked by treatment, given 0.2 μL water or none, returned to the nest, and their next-day foraging trips counted.
methods.evidence: Ants in the hydrated treatment group were marked with a different color of paint, and administered 0.2 μL of pure water (Millipore).

methods.name: Vapor Pressure Deficit regression of hydrated/unhydrated trip ratio
methods.description: Field temperature and humidity (iButton) were combined into VPD and regressed (linear vs quadratic, AIC/ANOVA) against the ratio of hydrated to unhydrated trips.
methods.evidence: A linear regression was performed with the ratio of hydrated to unhydrated foraging trips as the dependent variable and VPD as the independent variable.

methods.name: Laboratory desiccation assays on 74 foragers from 24 colonies
methods.description: Ants were held over Drierite at about 40 °C and weighed every 20 minutes, recording time to morbidity and death, blinded, to derive water loss rates and water contents.
methods.evidence: We used desiccation experi- ments to compare the physiological characteristics of N = 74 foragers from N = 24 colonies.

methods.name: Colony grouping by offspring success and foraging regulation
methods.description: Colonies were classified by prior parentage-analysis offspring status and by whether they reduce foraging in dry conditions, then compared with Wilcoxon and Chi-square tests.
methods.evidence: we classified colonies into two groups according to whether they reduced foraging activity in response to dry conditions

methods.name: PCA of five water-loss physiology measures
methods.description: Principal Component Analysis (factoextra in R) on water contents, times to morbidity and death, and area-independent water loss rate.
methods.evidence: We used Principle Component Analysis using the “factoextra” package64 to examine how forager water loss physiology was associated colony reproductive success

key_findings: Pooled across five colonies, hydrated ants made 1.18-fold more foraging trips than unhydrated nestmates (paired Wilcoxon p = 0.0006).
The hydration effect on foraging grew with desiccation risk (VPD), with a quadratic model fitting better than linear, supporting a non-linear effect.
Foragers from colonies that reduce foraging in dry conditions lost water faster and reached morbidity and death sooner, without differing in total or critical water content.
Surprisingly, colonies with offspring colonies had foragers with lower desiccation tolerance, which the authors suggest may reflect more cautious, water-conserving foraging.
The authors infer that an ant's threshold response to olfactory interactions that trigger foraging is influenced by its current hydration level.
key_findings_evidence: Pooling data from all colonies, hydrated ants made 1.18-fold more foraging trips than their unhydrated nestmates (3125 trips for hydrated versus 2652 trips for unhydrated ants from 5 colonies, paired sample Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p = 0.0006, Table 1).
This supports a non-linear effect of VPD on the influence of hydration on foraging trips.
Thus, differences among colonies in desiccation tolerance do not appear to be due to dif- ferences in initial water balance, but instead to differences in water loss rates across the cuticle.
Colonies with higher reproductive success, that had offspring colonies, had lower desiccation tolerance (Fig. 2).
indicates that an ant’s threshold response to olfactory interac- tions is influenced by its current hydration level.
